utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the record, could we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. Phillip Weiner for the Prosecution, with Sureta Chana, David Re, and Ana Vrljic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Peter Morrissey appearing for the Defence in this case, with co-counsel Mr. Mettraux, and also our legal assistant, Mr. Cengic, and Investigator Medina Delalic is present in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Halilovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this is a Status Conference of this case, during which we'll discuss some procedural matters and we are not going to deal with the substantive ones. There are several issues on our agenda. The first one is the resignation of Judge Szenasi. I'm very sorry to say that Judge Szenasi resigned last Friday because of health reasons, and it is very unfortunate for us to lose a Judge in the middle of the proceedings. In accordance with the Rule I believe 15 bis (C), the continuation of the proceedings can only be ordered with the consent of the accused. So I would like to turn to the Defence first, whether they had the opportunity to talk to their client about this matter and whether there's a consent from the accused on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is that, yes, we did have the opportunity to speak to Mr. Halilovic about it. He's very concerned not to delay proceedings here. And in short, Mr. Halilovic does consent to the replacement of the Judge and to the continuation of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now could I turn to Mr. Halilovic. Could you please confirm what Mr. Morrissey said just now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Morrissey has conveyed my position to you. I want the trial to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you agree that we'll continue the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any observations from the Prosecution on this very issue? Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to that specific issue, no, we would also like to continue with the case with regard to that part of it. We do have some other concerns, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Judge Szenasi's resignation is effective as of today, and the Trial Chamber will request the President to assign a new Judge to this case as early as possible. It is our -- it is also our intention to have this case to be continued. The next issue is about the 98 bis proceedings. The Trial Chamber wants to stress that the fact that Judge Szenasi is leaving the trial will not affect the Defence's ability to make 98 bis submissions. The Trial Chamber will do everything in its power that no disruption is caused due to Judge Szenasi's leaving and to enable the Defence to make its 98 bis submission, if the Defence so wishes. Mr. Morrissey, what's your position on this issue at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are concerned about the situation with respect to the 98 bis submission. The Defence is considering the possibility of not making any such submission. This was done in the case recently of Limaj, Bala, and Musliu. Now, that's a different Trial Chamber and the circumstances may be different, but we have some concerns both in form and substance about making a 98 bis submission in the current circumstances, and it's unfamiliar territory for everybody, I think, Your Honour. But very briefly, we think the Rules require that it be -- that the -- that the 98 bis submission be made before a Court consisting of three Judges, and all three of those Judges must -- or the new Judge must have certified his position in order to be able to deal with the 98 bis submissions. It seems to us that it just -- it would have artificial to require or to put a Judge in the position to answer that question without a significant adjournment of the proceedings, one which neither Mr. Halilovic nor the Chamber can really afford to happen. And for those reasons, we have a concern as to how a 98 bis proceeding would proceed with three Judges in the way that we think the Rules require. We've looked for alternative interpretations of the Rules. Frankly, we'll continue to look for those and consider this matter because it's a matter of significance in a number of ways. But that's our current view of it, that it's quite a difficult position at the moment for the third Judge to play any meaningful part, and that means that in effect the 98 bis submission would be one not proceeding in accordance with the Rules. In any event, the Defence is giving some consideration to whether or not it wishes to proceed with the 98 bis submission. We understand that in some respects these are -- this is a stage which can assist the Trial Chamber and we would not lightly not proceed with it. But those are the two things I -- two comments I have to make at this stage, that firstly we're not sure that as a matter of form it could be done; and secondly we are giving thought as a matter of substance we might choose not to do so in any event. And the final thing I wish to comment on is this: We think that if we're right in our interpretation of the Rules and the dangers that are posed, we think that significant time would have to pass by. And we understand there are a number of different pressures, not just the interests of Mr. Halilovic but other pressures of time in this case. And we're concerned that those pressures don't begin to squeeze upon the Defence case and the later preparations that follow upon that, so that any delay that happens now begins to impinge upon the ability of the Defence to prepare its case and to present its case accurately. That's not to say we're going to lead a lengthy case; we may well not. And part of our work in the next few weeks is bring it down and cut it down as much as possible. We really are going to try to trim this down greatly, but we don't want to be put in position where we have to do that because we're running out of time. And that's another reason why we're concerned about the 98 bis issue, this time pressure, which is nobody's fault, has now become a factor in the case. So that's what I can say in response to Your Honour's question at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think agree with you that it's nobody's fault that you give up this opportunity to make any submissions according to the 98 bis. Any response from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would just want to add that we're also very concerned about holding a 98 bis hearing without all members of the Bench being familiar with the record. The Rules, Rule 15 bis (D) indicates that a Judge cannot serve on the Bench until after they've certified that they've familiared [sic] himself or herself with the record of the proceedings. The spirit of this would seem to apply to both (C) and (D). It would not -- if one would think of it, it just wouldn't make sense under one -- even though it is written vaguely, to have under one section the Judge has to be familiar and under the other section the Judge does not have to be familiar. So the spirit of the Rules is that it does apply. And as a result, to hold a 98 bis hearing and get a 98 bis decision, we would have to have a panel, all three members of the panel being fully familiar. And if this Court wanted to move ahead immediately with the 98 bis, the Prosecution would request for appellate reasons, and there could be considerable appellate reasons, that the accused must consent -- or ask the accused's consent to a hearing without such certification that that Judge is familiar with the record. The Prosecution would want that to protect themselves. I mentioned this when I spoke with Mr. Morrissey prior to the hearing when we both discussed these matters. So the issue that we're both concerned about right now would be holding a 98 bis hearing with one Judge that is not familiar with the record and has not certified that he or she has done so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As I stated before, this Bench does not believe that Judge Szenasi's leaving will affect the submission of the 98 bis submissions. Anyway, the Rule 98 bis was recently amended and there are a lot of interpretations to this rule. And it will only have the Limaj case as a precedent before us. To my limited understanding, this Rule could be only invoked by submissions from the Defence. If there's no submissions from the Defence for the 98 bis, there's no such kind of proceedings. This is my limited understanding. Whether the Trial Chamber has the power to make a judgement on acquittal proprio motu is another matter, and it's still under the discussion and debate in this Tribunal. So at this stage, we'll not touch upon that very issue. But however, we believe that if there's no submissions from the Defence in accordance with the Rule 98 bis, we'll not invoke that procedure at this stage. So, Mr. Morrissey, could I confirm that you are going -- you are not going to file any submissions in according to the 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to formally reserve the position because we don't have a ruling at this stage on the record -- on the record of interview with Mr. Halilovic in 2001 and we have yet to hear the final witness. Can I indicate that as a matter of substance, that is very likely to be the position, that we will not do so. And therefore, we would not -- it's not necessary to plan for schedule for one to be heard. Of course, if anything should change, we would immediately advise the Chamber, and we understand that it's not a good idea for changes to occur, having indicated a course. I think it to -- very, very unlikely, but just as a matter of form I would wish to maintain a discretion to -- or at least leave to apply to do it subsequently, depending upon if something strange, for example, developed out of the evidence of Mr. Karic. I think it's unlikely, but formally speaking the Prosecution has not yet closed its case at this moment. But however, I can indicate that that is my intention at this point not to proceed with such -- not to invoke the procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course -- but, however, there must be a time limit on that. You cannot delay your decision, you know, until sometime very late because we have to guarantee expeditious trial of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, a time commitment can be fixed now, and that could be the morning after Mr. Karic, if that would be suitable to all. I can indicate that it's very unlikely that I would change my view, but at that moment I think it's fair to say the Prosecution case would be closed in every way, if I can indicate then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Well, the next issue is about the preparation of the Defence case. In our view, that the 98 bis proceedings does not affect the preparation of the Defence case. Pursuant to Rule 65 ter (G)(i), and (ii), the Trial Chamber shall order the Defence to file the list of the witnesses it intends to call and a list of exhibits and copies of exhibits the Defence intends to offer in its case. So I wonder at this stage whether the Defence is in the position to inform us whether -- at what time you could provide a 65 ter list. And the Trial Chamber would propose for the 13th of June. Do you think it's feasible at this stage, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is: Yes, I think we should aim for that. I think I -- I'm prepared to say it's feasible now. We are going to be sending people to Sarajevo shortly. And this case has had its developments, as all cases have, I suppose. And we have -- we now find ourselves in a somewhat different position than we were. One example is that we are now facing no expert testimony at all. In the past, we were. That will have an affect, and one would hope it would have an effect of shortening the case, because to the extent that we call expert evidence now, it would be focussed. It wouldn't be meeting a general expert opinion from the Prosecutor. It would be expert evidence an particular issues. So we think we can save time in that regard. Your Honours, again, if I may reserve the right to apply at a future time if we should find ourselves struggling. We think that setting an early deadline like that will help us to work out, frankly, and we're happy to aim for that. So may I just say, yes, that's an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I want to stress at this stage that the filing on the 13th of June is just a very preliminary filing, subject to the future changes and alternations because it's very difficult to predict the proceedings of the preparation of the case at this stage. And it is our intention to start the Defence case on the 20th of June. Is that agreeable to the parties? Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again, subject to what I said before, we think that would be in Mr. Halilovic's interest, to start as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Weiner, could I know your opinion on that? Do you think you have enough time to prepare for the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, as long as under (G)(i)(b) there is a summary of the facts upon which witness will testify is provided, and it's a full summary. We can then respond and deal with each of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And at this moment, we don't know how big is the Defence case yet. And what's the estimated length of the Defence case and whether there's any Rule 92 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, these matters are more volatile than my previous answers were as to the length of the Defence case. We do -- we have three categories of -- we have a number of different categories of witnesses that we have to see. At this stage it seems that a Defence case of approximately five weeks is possible. I want to make it clear that I prefer to run a case that is shorter than that. We aim to run a case that's shorter than that. Currently calling the witnesses that are on our list, I'm happy to say that I think it would take six weeks. I think it's realistic to say it will be reduced, and we wish it to be reduced further. But I want to say it's an unsatisfactory situation from the Prosecutor and Chamber's point of view that I can't be precise, but this case has had its changes and things have developed. Part of going to Sarajevo is to refine that. I myself will go there at some stage; others will go there before me to perform my other functions. So that the time estimate is volatile. It could be six weeks; it's likely to be five as things currently stand. We mean to reduce it further. I hope it to be shorter than that. As to the 92 bis situation, we intend to use that as much as we possibly can. There will be 92 bis witnesses. The way the Rules are structured now, it's necessary for the Defence to put material in mitigation of a plea, even if we're not -- even if we're ultimately acquitted, we're still obliged now to put certain material related to that. We're likely to put all of that as 92 bis if we can, and we'll see what the Prosecution say about that sort of thing. So there is likely that sort of material in 92 bis. There is other material that doesn't go to the movements or conduct of Mr. Halilovic himself, and we're likely to endeavour to put that sort of material as 92 bis. And it may be there's some material that's repetitive and we'll assess that. Depending on whether it's rational, if the Prosecutor would challenge that, we may put that as 92 bis as well. Can I indicate there is likely to be a substantial amount of material offered as 92 bis material. We think some of it would be -- the Prosecution would be content with and there may be some of it they would wish to cross-examine on. So that's the position. Again, that's one of the reasons I'm a little doubtful about the ultimate length of the Defence case, because that depends to some degree on what leave the Chamber grants to the Prosecution to cross-examine 92 bis witnesses, and that's a matter for argument. When the Prosecutors get our list, they can assess what they want to say about that. So that's my lengthy answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. To be on the safe side, we'll make it six weeks at least planned for the Defence case, which means we might sit in the first week of the recess, that is from 25th to 29th of July. We better make that reservation in advance so that we're prepared because it will affect dozens of people for their locations during that period. And according to Rule 93 ter, a pre-Defence conference would be held on the 17th June, so in order to discuss number of the witnesses the Defence want to call and how to shorten the estimated length of the Defence case. As for the expert witness, I would like to remind the Defence under Rule 94 bis the Prosecution has 30 days after the full statement of any expert witness has been disclosed to it within which to object, which means that if you would like to call an expert witness you had better furnish the statement of that expert in advance so that the Prosecution will have the opportunity or enough time to examine that report or might make any objections to the expert report. In the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, it is not quite clear what is exactly an expert report. I have to say -- well, I'm not going to comment in detail on this matter. I just remind the parties, be very careful with the expert report. Yes. And the last matter is that I wonder whether the Defence would like to make an opening statement on the first day of the start of its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the answer to that is, yes, we will wish to. I suspect that it is going to be a confined statement, but perhaps we'll just wait and see who we end up deciding to call, but I suspect it will be a confined opening statement, but, yes, I do wish to do that. I will give an estimate of the length of that, frankly, when I come back from Sarajevo, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- it won't be a monster. It won't go certainly outside of a day; it might not go outside of an hour, so it will be confined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The next issue is about the housekeeping matters and which may be related to the admission of the outstanding documents. On Thursday morning, we'll hear Mr. Karic's testimony via videolink conference. The scope and time is very limited for that procedure, so we could have some time left over on that day's sitting. We'll deal with some housekeeping matters, especially about the admission of outstanding documents. I believe that I asked both parties to submit their list of the documents for tendering as well as their objections to the document tendered by the other party. So I hope we could guide those submissions tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, at least before that housekeeping conference. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, are you referring to the documents of Bakir Alispahic or are you referring to any remaining documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First to the last witness, Bakir Alispahic, yeah. And secondly, I hope the Prosecution could go over all its files and to inform us whether in their case there are still some documents they would like to tender or we forgot to deal with it during the whole proceedings. It's a kind of housekeeping, you know, procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that is the same to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Well, I understood that was what Your Honour required. And I think in terms of the Prosecution there was the Alispahic documents and there were also some outstanding documents concerning the Witness Ramiz Delalic and there was an outstanding tape concerning -- arising from the witness Karavelic. So these are all matters. In relation to some of the Alispahic documents and the Karavelic ones, Mr. Re and I are going to speak. But you recall Mr. Re played a card in that discussion which I may find difficult to avoid in terms of Exhibit D390. So we'll certainly be speaking in that regard. It may be that we don't take the same attitude that we took in the past about it. The only question about that, Your Honour, is whether you wish submissions in writing about those things if we -- if we withdraw our objections to each other's exhibits. In any event, Your Honour, something's already been drafted. It hasn't been signed by me yet, but it's drafted, so you'll have that in the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If the parties could submit it in written form in a very concise format, that will be of great help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me, there is one matter to raise. It doesn't directly concern the Prosecution and at this stage it doesn't directly concern the Chamber, but I just need to make a record of it. Your Honours, at this stage the Defence has to enter into discussions with the registry concerning funding matters. And normally speaking, it's not something that Your Honour becomes involved with in any way. We just wish to note that we are in that phase, that because of the very tight time-lines that arise, sometimes if there isn't agreement or if there are difficulties that arise between registry and Defence counsel, it may be that -- that the registry would seek some assistance or guidance from elsewhere. I've indicated to the registry that I have no difficulty with them approaching the Chamber or its representatives at any time without first notifying me to verify any of the claims that I've made and the requests that I've made. Really, I just wish to put on record that I've done that so that in the future if the Chamber should be approached by registry in some form, that's with our authority. We want things to proceed clearly. But there is a difficulty that arises for the Defence and that is this: That if there are -- sorry, that our undertakings here to be able meet deadlines and our bona fide attempts to do that are going to depend on us having the full team. I'm basing that on -- that we'll be in a position to send investigators where we have to send them and to do what we have to do. I don't ask Your Honour to join in this discussion at this stage at all. I just mention that it is a factor, and it is a discussion that's going on now. And that should there be any difficulties, I just indicate I will come back and raise the matter, even though normally Your Honours do not provide a remedy directly here. Sometimes the Chamber is able to indicate what the Chamber thinks should happen or can indicate how a resolution might be reached. I've said all I have to say about that topic. The other thing that I would raise is that I just really wish to advise the Chamber of the effect of a delay on the Defence team. Your Honours have indicated time-lines which we think will avoid that problem, but if there are lengthy delays the Defence team consists of employees who are not employed permanently for a Defence generally but simply work for the Halilovic team and they're funded accordingly. If there were to be a delay, for example, of two months, those employed in the Halilovic team simply have to find other work, and that's the real world. Now, for myself, I can do that easily and the nature of my work is I can do that and come back and work again. If there was a delay of two months, it wouldn't compromise me; it would cause me difficulty but difficult is not a problem. For others, however, who have obligations elsewhere or who have to live and work and survive, it is a real issue and it is a genuine issue. So can I indicate that a lengthy delay would have the capacity to very adversely impact upon our team, and that indirectly would cause problems for the expeditious deciding of this case. It would affect Mr. Halilovic and affect all those who have a stake in the proceedings here, including the Tribunal itself. For that reason I also indicate that we feel ourselves obliged at all times to endeavour to avoid delays and it is very much not in our interest to have delays in that regard. I mention that because it's just a real-world situation we find ourselves in, and in the future if disasters happen, the Tribunal should know that that is a factor we have to wrestle with. It shouldn't be the case -- I don't mean any criticism of registry in this at all. It's just the way things are. That if there's a lengthy adjournment, that's the world in which I'm going to find myself in managing a team, which up to now has -- I'm very proud of and I don't wish to fall apart. So I mention that now, Your Honour, but at this stage the deadlines that Your Honours have set will avoid any difficulties like that. The other matter that arises from it is one -- this is a bit of forward thinking here. Should we finish the Defence case on or about the time when the -- when the recess takes place, then the Defence would be very keen to press ahead with the preparation of final submissions at final brief during that recess. That doesn't involve court staff or anything of that nature, but we're very keen to avoid a situation where there is, to use a phrase, downtime then for myself and Mr. Mettraux as well. We would be wanting to work and preparing at that time. That's a matter I will be indicating to the registry, and should they have any doubt about that it may be that the registry would wish to contact the Chamber and indicate -- and discover what the Chamber's view about it was. I mention it because it's going to arise in our discussions. None of that gives rise to remedy now, Your Honour. I'll stop. I thought I better put that on to record now because those are managerial issues we have to face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for bringing to our attention about the funding issues. At this stage I have to say that generally speaking this issue is within the mandate of the registrar. In the meantime, the -- it is also the responsibility for the Trial Chamber to guarantee a expeditious trial that is without any undue delay. So if there's any problem or if there's any difficulties on the part of the Defence concerning of these issues, I hope you could draw our attention to it and we'll do our best to facilitate the solving of this problem and to make the proceedings moving on. This is our responsibility, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And at this stage it's very difficult to predict whether there's any rebuttal and rejoinder procedures after the recess, so I will not make any comments on that issue. Yes. Are there any other matters on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I believe that's all for this Status Conference. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.51 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
